question: A propeller produces thrust fundamentally by:

options.text: Pushing directly against the ground through the air
Acting as a rotating aerofoil, each blade generating an aerodynamic force whose forward component is thrust, resulting from its angle of attack to the air it meets
Compressing air ahead of the aircraft, like a piston
Relying entirely on engine exhaust gas

explanation: Each propeller blade is an aerofoil moving through the air along a helical path, generating lift and drag exactly as a wing does. The component of that aerodynamic force acting forward, along the aircraft's direction of travel, is thrust.

question: A propeller blade's "geometric pitch" is the distance it would theoretically advance along its axis in one revolution, based purely on its blade angle, while the blade's actual angle of attack additionally depends on:

options.text: Engine RPM only, never on the aircraft's forward speed
The aircraft's forward speed, since the blade's actual angle of attack is the difference between its blade angle and the helical angle of its resultant motion through the air
Ambient temperature only
Nothing else — angle of attack and blade angle are always identical

explanation: A propeller blade moves through the air along a helical path combining its rotational speed and the aircraft's forward speed. Its actual angle of attack is the blade angle minus the helix angle of that resultant motion — which is why the same blade angle produces a different angle of attack (and different thrust) at different forward speeds.

question: "Torque reaction" describes the tendency of the aircraft to:

options.text: Yaw in the direction of propeller rotation
Roll in the opposite direction to the propeller's rotation, as a Newtonian reaction to the engine turning the propeller
Pitch nose-up at high power
Only occur with a twin-engine aircraft

explanation: By Newton's third law, as the engine applies torque to spin the propeller in one direction, an equal and opposite reaction torque tries to rotate the rest of the airframe in the other direction — felt mainly as a rolling tendency, especially noticeable at high power and low airspeed.

question: Gyroscopic precession from a spinning propeller, when a pitching or yawing force is applied to it, causes the resulting effect to appear:

options.text: At the same point the force was applied
Approximately 90 degrees further around the direction of rotation from where the force was applied
With no delay or offset at all
Only when the propeller is stationary

explanation: A spinning propeller behaves like a gyroscope: a force applied to try to tilt its axis in one direction actually produces a reaction roughly 90 degrees further around in the direction of rotation. This is why, for example, raising the tail of a taildragger during the takeoff roll can produce a yaw, rather than the pitching effect one might otherwise expect.

question: The "asymmetric blade effect" (P-factor), most noticeable at high angle of attack and high power, causes a yaw because:

options.text: Both propeller blades always produce identical thrust regardless of aircraft attitude
The descending blade meets the air at a higher angle of attack than the ascending blade, producing more thrust on that side of the disc
The propeller is mounted off-center on the engine
It only occurs with a feathered propeller

explanation: At a high angle of attack, the propeller disc is tilted relative to the oncoming airflow, so the descending blade meets the relative airflow at a greater angle of attack than the ascending blade and produces correspondingly more thrust. This asymmetric thrust across the disc yaws the aircraft — most pronounced at low airspeed and high power, such as during takeoff and initial climb.

question: The propeller's "slipstream effect" refers to the way its slipstream spirals backward around the fuselage and strikes the tail asymmetrically, typically producing:

options.text: A pitch-up tendency only
A yawing tendency, usually requiring rudder trim to counteract, particularly noticeable at high power and low airspeed
No aerodynamic effect on the tail at all
A rolling tendency only, never yaw

explanation: The propeller's slipstream twists into a helix as it travels rearward, and this rotating flow strikes the fin and rudder from one side more than the other, producing a yawing effect. It is strongest when the slipstream is fast relative to the aircraft's own forward speed — high power, low airspeed — the same conditions that also maximise P-factor and torque reaction.

question: Compared with a fixed-pitch propeller, a constant-speed propeller's main advantage is that it:

options.text: Never needs to be feathered
Automatically adjusts blade angle to maintain a selected RPM across a range of airspeeds and power settings, keeping the blades closer to their most efficient angle of attack throughout
Always produces less drag than a fixed-pitch propeller when stopped
Eliminates torque reaction entirely

explanation: A fixed-pitch propeller is aerodynamically efficient only over a narrow speed range, since its blade angle cannot change. A constant-speed propeller adjusts blade angle continuously to hold a chosen RPM, keeping the blades operating closer to their best angle of attack across a much wider range of airspeeds and power settings.

question: In a constant-speed propeller system, the governor responds to an increase in RPM above the selected value by:

options.text: Reducing engine power directly
Increasing propeller blade angle (coarsening pitch), which increases the load on the engine and brings RPM back down
Decreasing blade angle further
Shutting off fuel flow

explanation: The governor senses RPM and adjusts oil pressure to the propeller hub to change blade angle. If RPM rises above the selected value, the governor coarsens the blade angle, which increases the aerodynamic load the propeller presents to the engine and pulls RPM back down to the selected value — and does the reverse if RPM falls too low.

question: "Feathering" a propeller, typically after an engine failure, means rotating the blades so that:

options.text: They lie edge-on to the airflow, close to 90 degrees blade angle, minimising drag and windmilling tendency
They lie flat, face-on to the airflow, to maximise drag for a rapid descent
They rotate to a fixed low pitch angle for maximum thrust
They detach from the hub entirely

explanation: Feathering turns the blades so their chord line lies nearly parallel to the direction of flight — edge-on to the airflow — which minimises both the drag the stopped propeller presents and its tendency to keep windmilling, protecting a failed engine from further damage and preserving glide performance.

question: A propeller that is unfeathered and windmilling after an engine failure, compared with one that has been feathered, produces:

options.text: Less drag

Significantly more drag, because the blades continue to be driven by the airflow at an inefficient angle of attack, and it may also continue to turn — and potentially further damage — the failed engine
Exactly the same drag as a feathered propeller
Additional thrust instead of drag

explanation: A windmilling propeller is essentially acting as an unwanted, inefficient turbine, being driven by the airflow rather than driving the aircraft — producing substantially more drag than a feathered one, degrading glide performance and single-engine climb, and risking further mechanical damage to an already-failed engine.

question: A propeller's efficiency, the ratio of useful power output (thrust times velocity) to the engine's shaft power input:

options.text: Is constant at every combination of RPM and forward speed

Varies with the 'advance ratio' — forward speed relative to rotational speed — which is a key reason a fixed-pitch propeller cannot be equally efficient across a wide speed range, unlike a constant-speed propeller
Is always 100%, since a propeller cannot lose energy
Depends only on the number of blades

explanation: Propeller efficiency changes with the advance ratio because a fixed blade angle only presents its best angle of attack to the air at one particular combination of rotational and forward speed. Away from that point, efficiency falls off — which a constant-speed propeller avoids by continuously adjusting blade angle to stay near the optimum.

question: Adding more blades to a propeller of a given diameter, so it can absorb more engine power, compared with using fewer, wider blades, generally:

options.text: Always increases overall propeller efficiency, with no downside
Allows more power to be absorbed within a limited diameter — useful where ground clearance or blade tip speed limits diameter — often at some cost in efficiency compared with fewer, longer blades
Has no relationship to the power the propeller can absorb
Is only ever done to reduce noise, never to absorb more power

explanation: When diameter is limited — by ground clearance, blade tip speed, or other constraints — adding blades is a way to absorb more of a powerful engine's output without lengthening the blades. This can come at some cost to overall efficiency compared with an unconstrained design using fewer, longer blades.

question: Propeller blade tip speed is an important design limit mainly because:

options.text: It has no aerodynamic significance

As rotational speed and forward speed combine, the blade tips can approach or exceed the local speed of sound, causing the same compressibility losses — shockwaves, increased drag, reduced efficiency, extra noise — as on a wing at high Mach number
Tip speed only affects paint wear on the blades
It only matters for jet engines, not propellers

explanation: A propeller blade's tip moves through the air at the vector sum of its rotational speed and the aircraft's forward speed, and this combined speed can approach transonic values well before the aircraft itself does. The same compressibility effects that afflict a high-speed wing — shock formation, wave drag, reduced efficiency and sharply increased noise — apply to the blade tips.

question: On a hot day at a high-elevation airport (high density altitude), a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft's takeoff performance is typically degraded partly because:

options.text: The propeller bites into thinner air less effectively for a given RPM, producing less thrust, in addition to the engine itself producing less power
Propellers produce more thrust in thin air
Density altitude has no effect on propeller performance, only on wing lift
The propeller automatically increases its pitch to compensate

explanation: Thinner air at high density altitude reduces the mass flow a propeller can accelerate for a given RPM and blade angle, reducing thrust, on top of the naturally aspirated engine itself also producing less power in thin air — a double penalty on takeoff and climb performance that also compounds the wing's own reduced lift in thin air.

question: Propeller "solidity" is defined as the ratio of:

options.text: The total blade area to the area of the disc the propeller sweeps
Blade tip speed to the aircraft's forward speed
Engine RPM to propeller RPM
Propeller diameter to blade chord

explanation: Solidity is the ratio of the total blade area to the propeller disc area it sweeps. Higher solidity — from more blades, wider blades, or both — lets a propeller absorb more engine power and generate more thrust for a given diameter, generally at some cost in efficiency.

question: For a fixed maximum allowable blade tip speed, increasing a propeller's diameter requires:

options.text: Increasing RPM further, since diameter has no bearing on tip speed
Reducing RPM, since tip speed depends on both rotational speed and blade radius, and a larger radius reaches the same tip speed at a lower RPM
No change to RPM at all
Tip speed limits only apply to turboprop propellers, never piston ones

explanation: Blade tip speed is the vector sum of rotational speed (proportional to RPM times radius) and forward speed. Since tip speed rises with radius for a given RPM, a larger-diameter propeller must turn more slowly to stay under the same tip speed limit — one reason large-diameter propellers are typically geared to run more slowly than the engine driving them.

question: On a variable-pitch propeller with a "beta range", this range of blade angles is used mainly for:

options.text: In-flight cruise power management, exactly like the normal constant-speed governing range
Ground operations — from fine pitch through to reverse — where blade angle is commanded directly by the power lever rather than governed to hold a selected RPM
Feathering only
High-altitude cruise exclusively

explanation: Below the normal constant-speed governing range lies the beta range, used on the ground: blade angle is commanded directly rather than governed to maintain a set RPM, covering fine pitch for taxiing through to negative blade angles for reverse thrust.

question: A variable-pitch propeller produces reverse thrust by:

options.text: Reversing the direction the engine and propeller rotate
Rotating the blades to a negative blade angle, so their aerodynamic force now has a rearward component while the direction of rotation stays the same
Deploying a separate reversing duct, as on a turbofan
Simply reducing RPM toward zero

explanation: The propeller keeps turning in its normal direction; reverse thrust instead comes from rotating the blades through the beta range to a negative blade angle, so they now meet the air at an angle of attack that produces a rearward-acting force component, helping decelerate the aircraft after landing.

question: A "negative torque sensing" system on a turboprop engine exists to detect the condition where:

options.text: The propeller is producing too much forward thrust

The propeller, rather than being driven by the engine, is instead being driven by the airflow and tending to drive the engine — as after a power-section failure — and to respond automatically, typically by moving the blades toward feather
Engine RPM has exceeded its redline
Reverse thrust has been selected prematurely

explanation: Normally the engine drives the propeller; if the power section fails, the propeller can instead be driven by the airflow, windmilling and imposing an unwanted (negative) torque back on the engine. A negative torque sensing system detects this reversal and automatically commands the propeller toward feather, protecting the gearbox and reducing drag without waiting for crew action.

question: An armed autofeather system on a multi-engine turboprop is designed to:

options.text: Feather all propellers automatically at the top of climb
Automatically move a failing engine's propeller to feather, without pilot action, if power on that engine drops below a set threshold during a critical phase such as takeoff
Prevent any propeller from ever being feathered
Replace the need for a negative torque sensing system entirely

explanation: Armed for takeoff and initial climb, autofeather senses a significant, sudden loss of power on an engine and automatically drives that engine's propeller to feather, removing the very large drag of a windmilling propeller within seconds — faster than a crew could identify and action it manually — during exactly the phase of flight where that drag matters most.

question: A "tractor" propeller installation, mounted ahead of the wing or fuselage it drives, compared with a "pusher" installation:

options.text: Always produces less thrust for the same power
Draws relatively undisturbed air into the propeller disc, but its slipstream then passes back over the fuselage, wing and tail
Cannot be fitted with a constant-speed propeller
Eliminates torque reaction entirely

explanation: A tractor propeller sits ahead of the airframe, so its disc meets air that has not yet been disturbed by the fuselage or wing, which is aerodynamically clean. The cost is that its slipstream then washes back over the rest of the airframe, which is the direct cause of slipstream-induced yaw and the local lift changes it produces over the parts of the wing and tail it strikes.

question: A "pusher" propeller installation, mounted behind the wing or fuselage, typically:

options.text: Always achieves higher propeller efficiency than a tractor installation
Operates in air already disturbed by the fuselage or wing ahead of it, which can reduce propeller efficiency and increase vibration, though it keeps the slipstream from washing over the airframe
Cannot produce torque reaction
Is only ever used on gliders

explanation: Because the propeller disc is behind the airframe, it meets air that has already been slowed and disturbed by the fuselage or wing's own wake, which can reduce efficiency and increase vibration compared with a tractor installation. In exchange, the airframe itself sits in clean air ahead of the propeller, with no slipstream washing back over the wing or tail.

question: A mechanical "ground fine pitch stop" on a variable-pitch propeller exists to:

options.text: Allow the blades to move into reverse at any time during flight

Prevent the blades from moving below a set fine pitch angle while airborne, protecting against overspeed and excessive drag, while allowing that limit to be bypassed on the ground to reach beta and reverse range
Prevent the engine from ever exceeding idle power
Lock the propeller permanently at its most coarse pitch

explanation: The fine pitch stop limits how far the blades can move toward fine pitch in normal flight, protecting against a dangerous propeller overspeed and the very high drag an excessively fine blade angle would create. On the ground, a separate mechanism allows the blades to move past that stop into the beta and reverse range, where fine and negative pitch are wanted for ground handling.

question: Where a propeller's slipstream washes directly over part of a wing, the local effect on that section of wing is typically to:

options.text: Reduce the local airflow velocity, decreasing lift there
Increase the local airflow velocity over that section, increasing its local lift coefficient and, on some aircraft, delaying local stall in that area
Have no aerodynamic effect on the wing at all, only on the tail
Always cause that section of wing to stall first

explanation: A propeller accelerates the air passing through its disc, so any wing area sitting in that slipstream experiences a higher local airflow velocity than the rest of the wing. This increases the local lift generated there — most noticeable at low airspeed and high power — a separate effect from the slipstream's better-known tendency to yaw the aircraft by striking the tail asymmetrically.

question: Fitting counter-rotating propellers to a twin-engine aircraft — the two propellers turning in opposite directions — mainly serves to:

options.text: Increase the total thrust available beyond what same-rotation propellers could produce

Make the asymmetric effects, such as P-factor, of the two engines mirror-image opposites, so neither engine produces a consistently larger yawing moment when inoperative — removing the concept of a "critical engine"
Eliminate torque reaction on both engines
Allow the aircraft to be flown with no rudder input after an engine failure

explanation: On a conventional twin with both propellers rotating the same direction, one engine's failure produces a larger yawing moment than the other's because asymmetric effects like P-factor add to the moment arm on one side and subtract on the other. Counter-rotating propellers make those effects mirror images of each other, so both engines produce the same yawing moment if they fail — there is no longer a "worse" engine to lose.

question: On a conventional twin-engine aircraft where both propellers rotate in the same direction, the "critical engine" is defined as the engine whose failure:

options.text: Produces the least reduction in controllability and performance
Produces the greater reduction in controllability and performance, typically because its loss removes the propeller whose asymmetric thrust effects were creating the larger adverse yawing moment
Is always the left-hand engine, regardless of propeller rotation direction
Only matters for single-engine aircraft

explanation: With same-rotation propellers, the two engines are not aerodynamically equal contributors to yaw: because of effects such as P-factor, one engine's descending blade sits further from the aircraft's centreline than the other's, giving it a longer moment arm. The engine whose failure removes the more significant of these effects — leaving the worse controllability and performance problem — is the critical engine.

question: VMCA (air minimum control speed) is defined, for a given configuration, as the minimum speed at which:

options.text: The aircraft can be flown with both engines at idle power

Directional control can be maintained with the critical engine suddenly made inoperative and the remaining engine at maximum takeoff power, using a defined maximum bank angle and no more than a specified rudder input
The aircraft will not stall under any circumstances
All propellers must be feathered

explanation: VMCA is a defined, tested speed: with the critical engine failed and the other engine developing maximum takeoff power, it is the minimum speed at which the test pilot can still keep the aircraft on a straight heading, within a specified bank angle, using no more than a stated amount of rudder — below it, directional control cannot be assured.

question: Compared with its certificated value, VMCA on a given twin will generally be higher if:

options.text: The centre of gravity is further forward than certificated
The centre of gravity is further aft than certificated, since this shortens the moment arm the rudder has to counter the asymmetric yawing moment
The failed engine's propeller has been feathered rather than left windmilling
The aircraft is operating at a higher density altitude than certificated

explanation: VMCA is tested with a defined, forward centre of gravity, because a more aft CG reduces the rudder's moment arm and therefore its authority to counter the asymmetric yaw from the operating engine, raising VMCA. Conversely, feathering the failed propeller removes its drag and reduces the yawing moment, and reduced power available at higher density altitude lowers the asymmetric thrust — both tend to lower VMCA rather than raise it.

question: A propeller's aerodynamic efficiency — thrust multiplied by true airspeed, divided by shaft power absorbed — at the zero-forward-speed static condition used at the start of a takeoff roll is:

options.text: At its maximum, since thrust is highest at this point
Zero by definition, even though the propeller is producing substantial static thrust, because the useful power output term is zero when true airspeed is zero
Impossible to calculate at zero forward speed
Always exactly 100%, since no forward drag exists yet

explanation: Propeller efficiency is useful power output — thrust multiplied by true airspeed — divided by shaft power delivered. At zero forward speed that product is zero no matter how much static thrust is produced, so efficiency is zero by definition at the very start of the takeoff roll, rising rapidly as forward speed builds even though static thrust itself is often near its maximum value.

question: A normally aspirated (non-turbocharged) piston engine driving a fixed-pitch propeller will typically find that, as altitude increases:

options.text: Maximum attainable RPM increases, since thinner air offers the propeller less resistance to turn, even though the engine itself is producing less power
Maximum attainable RPM decreases at exactly the same rate the engine's power falls
RPM is completely unaffected by altitude
RPM can only ever be limited by a governor, never by altitude

explanation: A fixed-pitch propeller's load on the engine depends on the density of the air it turns in; in the thinner air of altitude it offers less resistance, letting the same power setting spin it to a higher RPM than at sea level, even as the naturally aspirated engine's own maximum power output falls with altitude — the two effects work against each other rather than cancelling exactly.

question: Many turboprop and some geared piston engines drive their propeller through a reduction gearbox mainly because:

options.text: It allows the engine to run at a higher, more efficient RPM while keeping the propeller's own RPM — and therefore blade tip speed — low enough to avoid compressibility losses
It increases propeller RPM above engine RPM
It has no effect on propeller tip speed
It exists solely to reduce engine noise

explanation: A gas turbine in particular runs most efficiently at a much higher RPM than a propeller can usefully turn at without its blade tips approaching the speed of sound. A reduction gearbox lets the engine run at its own efficient RPM while turning the propeller at a much lower RPM, keeping tip speed — and the compressibility losses that come with it — within acceptable limits.

question: A propeller blade is typically twisted along its length, with a coarser blade angle at the root than at the tip, mainly because:

options.text: It looks more aerodynamic

Rotational speed increases from root to tip, so without twist the outer sections would meet the air at a much smaller angle of attack than the inner sections; twist keeps angle of attack more consistent along the blade's span
It reduces the total weight of the blade
It has no aerodynamic purpose, only a structural one

explanation: Every point along a propeller blade moves at a different rotational speed — faster toward the tip, slower toward the root — while the aircraft's forward speed is the same for the whole blade. Twisting the blade so the angle progressively decreases from root to tip compensates for this, keeping each section closer to its own most efficient angle of attack rather than the tip stalling or the root angle of attack being far too high.

question: A synchrophasing system on a multi-engine, multi-propeller aircraft is used to:

options.text: Automatically feather a propeller after an engine failure
Hold the propellers at matched RPM and a set relative blade phase angle to each other, reducing the beat-frequency noise and vibration that unsynchronised propellers produce
Reverse all propellers simultaneously on landing
Deliberately increase the RPM of one propeller above the others

explanation: Propellers that are close in RPM but not identical produce a distinctive, fluctuating beat noise and vibration as their blades pass in and out of phase with each other. A synchrophasing system fine-tunes each propeller's RPM and controls the relative angular position between them, holding a fixed phase relationship that noticeably reduces cabin noise and airframe vibration.

question: After an engine failure causes a loss of its own oil pressure, a propeller that still succeeds in feathering typically relies on:

options.text: The failed engine somehow regenerating oil pressure on its own
A separate reserve, such as an accumulator or the still-operating engine's own oil supply, dedicated to driving the feathering mechanism independently of the failed engine's own oil pressure
Gravity alone acting on the blades
The propeller being unable to feather once its engine's oil pressure is lost

explanation: Many constant-speed propeller systems normally use engine oil pressure to control blade angle, which would be lost along with the failed engine's own oil pressure at the worst possible moment. To feather reliably after such a failure, the system provides a separate source of pressure — such as a spring-loaded or nitrogen-charged accumulator, or a supply routed from the still-running engine on a twin — dedicated to driving the blades to feather independently of the failed engine's own oil.

question: Some aircraft placard a particular propeller RPM range as unsuitable for sustained (continuous) operation, mainly because:

options.text: That RPM range wastes the most fuel
That RPM range coincides with a natural vibration frequency of the propeller, engine mount or airframe, and continuous operation there risks a damaging resonance building up over time
It is illegal to operate below the aircraft's maximum RPM at any time
It only affects the electrical system, not the structure

explanation: A propeller-engine combination has natural resonant frequencies, and running continuously at an RPM that excites one of them can allow vibration amplitude to build up over time, risking fatigue damage to the propeller, engine mounting or nearby airframe structure. The fix is not to avoid that RPM outright, but to placard it against sustained operation while allowing a brief transit through it.

question: In cruise flight, a constant-speed propeller is typically operated at a coarser blade angle and lower RPM than during the takeoff roll, mainly because:

options.text: Coarse pitch and low RPM together give the best fuel efficiency for the modest thrust needed to maintain cruise speed, since the high angle of attack that fine pitch and high RPM provide is not needed for maximum static thrust
Coarse pitch always produces more total thrust than fine pitch at any airspeed
RPM has no effect on fuel consumption
Cruise flight requires the maximum RPM available, the same as takeoff

explanation: Takeoff needs maximum thrust, which a fine blade angle and high RPM deliver even though this is aerodynamically inefficient. In cruise, far less thrust is needed to maintain speed, so a coarser blade angle at a lower, more fuel-efficient RPM keeps the blades near their best angle of attack for the higher forward speed and lower power required, trading maximum thrust capability for efficiency.

question: A fixed-pitch propeller's blade angle must be chosen as a single compromise value because it cannot adjust in flight, which means an aircraft fitted with one:

options.text: Achieves its best propeller efficiency at every combination of RPM and airspeed simultaneously

Can be optimised for good climb performance or for good cruise efficiency, but not fully for both — a "climb" propeller sacrifices some cruise efficiency, and a "cruise" propeller sacrifices some climb performance
Cannot produce thrust at all in cruise flight
Is always more efficient overall than a constant-speed propeller

explanation: Because a fixed-pitch propeller's single blade angle can only be near-optimal at one particular combination of airspeed and RPM, the manufacturer or owner must choose which flight regime to favour. A propeller pitched fine for strong static and climb performance will be somewhat inefficient at cruise speed, and one pitched coarser for efficient cruise will give a longer takeoff roll and a shallower climb.

question: A propeller's "disc loading" is defined as:

options.text: The thrust produced divided by the area of the disc the propeller sweeps
The total weight of the propeller blades
The number of blades divided by propeller diameter
Maximum RPM divided by disc area

explanation: Disc loading is thrust divided by the swept disc area. A propeller of larger diameter turning more slowly can produce the same thrust at a lower disc loading than a smaller, faster-turning one, generally with better propulsive efficiency, though at the cost of the ground clearance and practical diameter limits covered elsewhere.

question: In most constant-speed propeller systems, a failure that causes a complete loss of governing oil pressure will tend to drive the propeller toward:

options.text: Feather, protecting the engine automatically
Fine pitch, risking an overspeed, since a spring and/or counterweights typically drive the blades toward fine pitch by default when governing oil pressure is lost
Reverse pitch
Whatever blade angle it happened to be at, with no tendency to move

explanation: A typical constant-speed hub uses oil pressure, opposed by springs or counterweights, to hold a coarser blade angle; losing that oil pressure lets the springs or counterweights win, driving the blades toward fine pitch by default. Fine pitch offers little resistance to rotation, so the engine can accelerate toward a dangerous overspeed unless power is reduced immediately — a different failure mode from the loss of a failed engine's own oil pressure feathering system described elsewhere, which most designs protect against with a separate mechanism.

question: An in-flight restart of a failed engine using "windmill" relighting relies on:

options.text: The starter motor exclusively, with the propeller stopped
Airflow through the still-unfeathered, windmilling propeller continuing to turn the engine fast enough to permit relighting, without needing the electric starter
The propeller being fully feathered throughout the restart attempt
Ground personnel manually turning the propeller

explanation: If the propeller has not been feathered, the airflow keeps driving it — and through it, the engine — as the aircraft continues to fly. Provided the resulting windmilling RPM is high enough, this alone can supply the rotation needed to attempt a relight without engaging the electric starter, which is one reason a crew might deliberately delay feathering if a prompt restart looks likely.
